input:
Start-up

It should be understood at the outset that the pressure relief valve covered by this chapter is a vitally important protective device, and that the operator in charge of the protected equipment has charge of the valve as well. The function of the valve is to open automatically when the pressure reaches the set pressure, to discharge fluid until the pressure has fallen, and subsequently to reseat itself, without any intervention on the part of the operator. The instructions in this chapter, which relate to start-up, normal operation, alarms, and shutdown, are designed to ensure that the valve remains capable of performing this function, and they should be followed in the sequence presented, the sequence being discontinued at any point where a check is not satisfied until the fault has been reported and cleared.

Attention should be directed first of all to the discharge side. The discharge line should be traced from the valve outlet to the safe discharge point, and it should be established that the line is open along the whole of its length, free from caps, plugs, blanks, and shut valves, and sound at every joint. Attention should then be turned to the inlet side, where, where an inlet isolation valve has been fitted, that valve should be opened fully and secured open. The valve body and both flanges should be examined for damage, distortion, corrosion, and staining indicative of past leakage, and the pressure gauge on the protected equipment should be checked to ensure that it is readable, undamaged, and live on the equipment rather than shut off from it.

The protected equipment should be brought up to pressure slowly, in accordance with its own start-up procedure, the operator standing where the gauge can be observed and the outlet heard. When the normal operating pressure has been reached, the equipment should be held steady and the state of the valve confirmed, there being no discharge at the outlet, no hissing sound indicative of passing fluid, and no leakage at either of the flanges. An entry should then be made in the operating log, recording that the inlet is open, the discharge line proved, and the valve shut at the normal operating pressure.

If the valve is found to be passing or lifting during the course of this initial pressurisation, no attempt should be made to coax it back by hand, and the spring and adjuster should be left entirely untouched. The pressure should be brought down if the discharge fails to stop, and the valve should be reported to the supervisor so that it can be examined under permit, the equipment remaining without its full protection until the valve has been passed fit.

Normal operation

Under normal operating conditions, the relief valve is to be found in the shut condition, fitted to equipment that is live, with the equipment being operated at a pressure below the set pressure of the valve. The responsibility of the operator under these circumstances is essentially to ensure that any change in the condition of the valve is noticed at an early stage, as with a valve becoming audible, a joint staining, or an outlet showing signs of flow.

The valve should be included in every round. The pressure gauge on the protected equipment should be read and the reading noted against the normal operating band for the equipment, while the valve, its flanges, and the first length of discharge line are inspected for leakage, corrosion, and damage from nearby work. The outlet should be listened at for passing and examined for the marks a discharge leaves behind, including deposits, staining, and icing. The round should be written up in the operating log regardless of whether or not anything of note has been found, so that a record exists of the watch kept.

It is essential that the valve is not given any work to do during normal operation. The valve should not be cracked open in order to test it, it should not be eased with a lever, and it should not be used to control the equipment pressure, since it is a protective device, not a control valve, and a hand-opened valve may not reseat correctly. The ground round the valve and the discharge outlet should be kept clear, for access and for a discharge to escape safely, and paint should be kept off the valve entirely, the nameplate remaining readable and the spring housing free of paint that might trap moisture. Any damage, corrosion, leakage, or passing that is discovered should be reported to the supervisor on the same shift.

Three rules are applicable throughout the whole of the operating period. The inlet isolation valve is not to be closed while pressure is held within the protected equipment. The discharge outlet is not to be obstructed, even merely to silence a passing valve. The set pressure is not to be altered, and no instruction to alter it is to be accepted other than under a maintenance permit with the valve removed from the plant, the three rules together ensuring that, should the pressure rise beyond the limit, the valve is connected, unobstructed, and set as it was set on the test bench.

Alarms

Two alarms fitted on the protected equipment involve the relief valve, each with its own course of action. In neither instance does the action that is required involve work being carried out on the valve itself, the relevant tools being the gauge, the normal means of cutting the pressure at its source, and the withdrawal of personnel from the discharge area.

Protected equipment pressure high

This alarm indicates that the pressure in the protected equipment has climbed towards the set pressure, and that the valve may lift at any moment. The alarm should first be checked against the local pressure gauge. The pressure should then be cut at its source by the normal means applicable to the equipment, the inflow, the firing, or the feed driving the pressure up being stopped. The discharge outlet area should be cleared and kept clear, and if the pressure continues to climb, personnel should move out of the line of the discharge, the supervisor should be informed, and the valve should be left to lift and reseat without interference. After the pressure has fallen and become steady, the event should be logged and the valve reported for inspection.

Relief valve discharging

This alarm indicates that fluid is passing out of the discharge, whether from a full lift of the valve or from the valve passing heavily. Personnel near the outlet should be moved away from the discharge and kept away, and the pressure gauge on the protected equipment should be watched, a satisfactory lift being characterised by a falling pressure. The valve should not be approached, no attempt should be made to shut it, and the discharge should not be blocked to stop the noise or the loss. If the pressure fails to fall, the supervisor should be informed without delay and the emergency procedure for the equipment followed. After the discharge has ended and the valve has reseated, the lift should be logged and the valve reported for examination before it is relied upon again.

Shutdown

The relief valve should be retained in service for the whole of the shutdown, until such time as the protected equipment has been proved to be empty of pressure. The work of the valve is not completed merely because the pressure source has been cut off, since heat soak or a passing isolation can cause the pressure to rise again, and it is against such eventualities that the valve continues to protect for as long as it remains connected and unobstructed.

The pressure should be run down in accordance with the shutdown procedure for the protected equipment, and the equipment proved empty of pressure, first on its gauge and secondly at its vent or drain, before the valve isolation is touched. In cases in which the valve is to be removed for the purposes of bench testing or renewal, the inlet isolation valve should be closed only after this proof has been obtained, following which the drain or vent between the isolation and the valve should be opened and that length proved empty, that short length being proved as carefully as the vessel itself. No flange bolt should be loosened until both proofs have been made and recorded.

The valve itself is removed under a maintenance permit, the duty of the operator concluding with the hand-over. The removal should be logged, together with the equipment that the valve guarded and its proved state, and the open flange that remains following the removal should be blanked. Equipment standing without its relief valve is not to be pressurised, and no start-up should be permitted on such equipment until a proved valve has been fitted once again or a protective arrangement that has been approved for the purpose has been installed in its place.

In summary: the discharge and the inlet are to be proved before pressure is raised, the valve watched and left alone in operation, its two alarms answered by cutting the pressure and clearing the discharge area, and the valve kept in service at shutdown until the equipment is proved empty.
target:
Start-up

You have charge of the pressure relief valve whenever the equipment it protects is in your care. The valve is the last protection on that equipment: it opens at the set pressure, discharges until the pressure falls, and reseats itself, all without action from you. The start-up, normal operation, alarm, and shutdown instructions in this chapter keep the valve able to do that work. Follow them in the order given, and stop the sequence at any point where a check fails, until the fault has been reported and cleared.

Start with the discharge side. Walk the discharge line from the valve outlet to the safe discharge point and satisfy yourself that the line is open along its whole length, free of caps, plugs, blanks, and shut valves, and sound at every joint. Move then to the inlet: where an inlet isolation valve is fitted, open it fully and secure it open. Examine the valve body and both flanges for damage, distortion, corrosion, and staining from past leaks. Last, check the pressure gauge on the protected equipment: it must be readable, undamaged, and live on the equipment, not shut off from it by a closed cock.

Bring the protected equipment up to pressure slowly, by its own start-up procedure, and stand where you can see the gauge and hear the valve outlet as the pressure rises. At the normal operating pressure, hold the equipment steady and confirm the state of the valve: no discharge at the outlet, no hiss of passing fluid, no leak at either flange. Enter the start-up in the operating log, noting that the inlet is open, the discharge line proved, and the valve shut at the normal operating pressure.

A valve that passes or lifts during this first pressurisation is not to be coaxed back by hand. Keep your hands off the spring and the adjuster, bring the pressure down if the discharge does not stop, and report the valve to the supervisor for examination under permit. The equipment is without its full protection until the valve has been passed fit, and the log entry must say so.

Normal operation

Normal operation for the relief valve is a shut valve on live equipment. The equipment runs below the set pressure, and the valve waits. Your task in this state is to notice change early: a valve that was tight and becomes audible, a joint that was dry and begins to stain, an outlet that was cold and shows signs of flow.

Make the valve part of every round. Read the pressure gauge on the protected equipment and note the reading against the equipment's normal operating band. Look over the valve, both flanges, and the first length of discharge line for leakage, corrosion, and damage done by passing work. Listen at the outlet for passing, and look for the marks that discharge leaves behind it: deposits at the outlet, staining, eroded paint, icing on cold service. Write the round up in the operating log whether or not anything was found, so that the record shows the watch kept on the valve as plainly as on any other item of the plant.

Do not give the valve work to do in normal operation. Do not crack it open to test it, do not ease it with a lever, and do not use it to control the equipment pressure; it is a protective device, not a control valve, and a valve opened by hand may not reseat on its seat afterwards. Keep the ground round the valve and the discharge outlet clear for access and for a discharge to escape safely. Keep paint off the valve entirely: the nameplate must stay readable and the spring housing must stay free of paint that traps moisture. Report damage, corrosion, leaks, and passing to the supervisor on the shift on which you find them.

Three rules bind you for the whole period of operation. You do not close the inlet isolation valve while the protected equipment holds pressure. You do not obstruct the discharge outlet, even to silence a passing valve. You do not alter the set pressure, and you accept no instruction to do so outside a maintenance permit with the valve off the plant. Each rule protects the same point: when the pressure rises beyond the limit, the valve must be connected, open-mouthed, and set as it was set on the test bench.

Alarms

Two alarms fitted on the protected equipment involve the relief valve, and each has its own action. In neither case is the action work on the valve. Your tools are the pressure gauge, the normal means of cutting the pressure at its source, and the withdrawal of people from the discharge area.

Protected equipment pressure high

The pressure in the protected equipment has climbed towards the set pressure and the valve may lift at any moment. Check the alarm against the local pressure gauge first. Then cut the pressure at its source by the normal means for the equipment: stop the inflow, the firing, or the feed that is driving the pressure up. Clear the discharge outlet area and keep it clear. If the pressure still climbs, get out of the line of the discharge, tell the supervisor, and leave the valve to lift and reseat on its own. Once the pressure is down and steady, log the event and report the valve for inspection; it has worked near its limit and is checked before the equipment runs unrestricted again.

Relief valve discharging

Fluid is passing out of the discharge, either from a full lift or from a valve passing heavily. Move yourself and anyone near the outlet away from the discharge and keep them away. Watch the pressure gauge on the protected equipment: a healthy lift shows the pressure falling. Do not go to the valve, do not try to shut it, and do not block the discharge to stop the noise or the loss. If the pressure does not fall, tell the supervisor at once and follow the emergency procedure for the equipment. After the discharge ends and the valve has reseated, log the lift and report the valve for examination before it is trusted for a further period of service.

Shutdown

Keep the relief valve in service for the whole of the shutdown until the protected equipment is proved empty of pressure. The valve's work is not finished when the pressure source is cut: heat soak, a passing isolation, or liquid warming in a shut vessel can raise the pressure again, and the valve guards against each of them for as long as it stays connected and unobstructed.

Run the pressure down by the shutdown procedure for the protected equipment. Prove the equipment empty of pressure on its gauge and again at its vent or drain before you touch the valve's isolation. Where the valve is to come off for bench testing or renewal, close the inlet isolation valve only after that proof. Open the drain or vent in the pipe length between the isolation and the valve, and prove that length empty as well: it is short, it is easy to overlook, and it holds pressure exactly as the vessel did. Loosen no flange bolt on the valve until both proofs have been made and recorded.

The valve itself comes off under a maintenance permit; your duty ends with the hand-over. Log the removal, the equipment the valve guarded, and the proved state of that equipment. Blank the open flange that the removal leaves. Treat equipment standing without its relief valve as equipment that must not be pressurised, and allow no start-up on it until a proved valve is fitted again or a protective arrangement approved for the purpose has been installed in its place.

In restatement: prove the discharge and the inlet before pressure is raised, watch the valve and leave it alone while the equipment runs, answer its two alarms by cutting the pressure and clearing the discharge area, and keep it in service until the protected equipment is proved empty at shutdown.
